Before a database writes a change to its primary storage, it writes the change to its write-ahead log. This is a record of all of the changes that have been made to the database since the last checkpoint. During a crash, when the database is shut down abruptly, the primary storage may be inconsistent, while the write-ahead log remains consistent. After the crash, the database can be recovered by redoing all of the changes recorded in the write-ahead log. This process is known as "replaying" the log. By replaying the log, the database can restore its primary storage to a consistent state, allowing it to continue operating as if the crash had never occurred. This approach ensures that the database remains consistent despite the possibility of failures.
The write-ahead log is a key component of a database's crash recovery mechanism. It serves as a record of all the changes made to the database, allowing the database to recover from a crash by replaying the log and redoing the changes. This ensures that the database remains consistent and can continue operating after a crash. The log is also used during normal operation to ensure durability of transactions, by waiting for the log records to be written to disk before considering a transaction complete.
